prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of who trades, how resources are reallocated and how countries gain from trade

statement.case_for: In my opening I ranked B006 first and B001 second. After reading the openings I now put B001 first, and I regard the gap between the two as small. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) moved trade from sector-level to firm-level analysis. They supplied a new, testable channel for gains from trade (selection and reallocation), and the export-versus-FDI sorting result has been checked repeatedly in firm microdata. This is the kind of practically useful theory tied closely to data that I think the Committee has valued. The core papers are more than twenty years old, so the record is mature. The attribution to Helpman and Melitz is also unusually clean. Melitz is the originator of the baseline model. Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition foundations and his role in the FDI margin make him a natural co-laureate. I do not treat the large number of colleagues who proposed the same pair as evidence of merit. The case rests on the substance above and on the tighter discovery boundary compared with the main alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the edges of the discovery. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions and are not credited on this ballot entry. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is also left out of a two-person award. The baseline Melitz model's sharp predictions are rejected in detail, so the lasting contribution is the framework and its extensions rather than the original specification. The award would also sit in a field that Krugman's 2008 prize partly covered, and the Committee may judge the incremental step to be smaller than a first-order reading suggests.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranked B006 third and said that bundling demand estimation, production-function estimation and dynamic games makes the boundary of the B006 discovery fuzzy. She also said methodological prizes may be weighed against substantive findings.
responses.response: I think this is a fair criticism and it is a main reason I moved B006 down. In my opening I treated the BLP demand strand and Pakes's dynamic-model strand as one achievement. A prize would have to say clearly whether it rewards BLP demand estimation or the broader structural-IO toolkit. With a three-name cap, that choice is harder to defend than the Helpman-Melitz pairing. I do not accept that a method cannot qualify. BLP changed practice in antitrust, trade and health economics, and I would still support B006 as an alternative.

responses.point: Friberg ranked B006 second and asked whether Bresnahan should displace one of the three names. He also noted that the Committee may see the B006 contribution as methodological rather than a discovery about the economy.
responses.response: I agree that the Bresnahan question is open, and that is another reason I am no longer confident in the BLP-trio configuration. Bresnahan's independent contributions to empirical IO and the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core cannot both be fully credited within three names. On the methods-versus-discovery point I disagree somewhat. Structural IO methods have revealed facts about market power and welfare that reduced-form work could not. But Friberg's concern about how the citation is framed is legitimate, and it strengthens the case for a cleaner B001 citation.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B001 first. He argued that Melitz is central, that Helpman is the natural co-recipient, and that Redding is the more derivative third name, so two laureates give the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I largely agree on the two-name configuration, but I would qualify the reasoning. Calling Redding derivative understates his quantitative and spatial work, which is substantial. My reason for omitting him is narrower: that work is a later extension, not the origin of the selection result. I would also not dismiss the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line as easily as the list suggests. If the Committee wants to cover the full firm-level trade lineage, the two-name award is vulnerable on exactly that point.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B001 first. He noted that some predictions of the baseline model are rejected in detail, although the framework has been widely extended. He also asked how credit should be divided with the quantitative trade tradition (B037).
responses.response: I take the first point as a real qualification and have put it in my case against. The citation should credit the framework of selection and reallocation, not the baseline model's specific predictions. On B037, B037 is not on the shortlist, so I only note that the quantitative-trade lineage is a possible competing way to frame the field and not an argument against B001's core.

responses.point: Krusell and Enflo both ranked B034 second. They argued that Kiyotaki-Moore is the clean, identifiable origin of the collateral-constraint credit-cycle mechanism.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution argument and keep B034 as an alternative. My reservation is the one Enflo and Fredriksson also raise. The mechanism overlaps thematically with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and direct empirical validation of the collateral channel is mixed. For that reason I place it behind B001 and B006.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers to credit the firm-heterogeneity strand to Helpman and Melitz alone, or to widen it to Redding or to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are outside the credited list.
Whether Helpman is better paired with Grossman (B047) in a different trade citation. B047 is not on the shortlist, so I cannot assess it here.

How to weigh B006's methodological breadth against its fuzzy discovery boundary, including whether Bresnahan should be credited. My assessment rests on general knowledge and not independently verified sources.
Whether the 2022 prize makes B034 redundant or complementary.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors and research areas (corporate finance, venture capital and private equity, carbon pricing) do not overlap with any credited name on the shortlisted entries. I have long committee overlap with several colleagues, but that is not a disqualifying connection.
